A1.justification: Despite the changed title and organization, both PDFs describe the same reward-learning framework, optimization approach and toy simulation. Their main texts, equations, figures, tables and appendices support a reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 Section 5.3 and Appendix C.5 report original simulations, numerical optimizer outputs, convergence plots and validation through feasible-set discretization.

after.justification: v2 Section 6 and Appendix F retain the original simulation results, optimization trajectories and discretization validation.

M1.justification: Rob-ReL retains the RF-Express exploration, primal-dual optimization and extrema/midpoint construction. It now estimates the two target-policy visitation distributions and incorporates them into the objective, whereas v1's implemented formulation assumes them known. Direct scalar prediction and the general minimax decision formulation already appear in v1 Proposition 5.6 and Appendix C.3.

E1.justification: Both evaluate the same toy road environment, policy-preference task and six feedback constraints. The additional application examples in v2 are mathematical illustrations, not newly evaluated datasets or scenarios.

E2.justification: Both retain the comparison with arbitrary feasible rewards and the discretization reference used to validate optimization. No named reward-learning algorithm is newly benchmarked; the expanded citations do not constitute experimental comparators.

E3.justification: The stated target statistic changes from J(pi2)-J(pi1) in v1 Section 5.1 to J(pi1)-J(pi2) in v2, without changing the named policies. This changes the reported preference direction, but does not establish a rerun. The horizon, feedback, exact-model assumption, 1,200 iterations and 0.01 step size are retained.

E4.justification: The optimizer trajectories and objective curves in Figures 12–13, and the discretization validation in Figure 14, are retained from v1 Appendix C.5 in v2 Appendix F. No new ablation, sensitivity or empirical robustness analysis is reported.

E5.justification: Neither version reports empirical repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. Changes to probabilistic sample-complexity proofs concern theory rather than empirical uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: The main numerical values remain: extrema -0.62 and 1.02, prediction 0.2, target difference 0.39, and worst-case errors 0.82 and 1.64. However, v2 associates the positive difference with the opposite policy ordering and no longer prints the learned reward vector [0.62, 0.48, 0.02], although its plotted point remains. No performance improvement is established.

T1.justification: v2 Theorem 5.3 and Appendix E revise the principal guarantee to include estimated target-policy occupancies and change the iteration-complexity bound. The concentration lemma changes its dependence from 1/epsilon_EST to 1/epsilon_EST squared. v2 also adds formal application losses and a maximum-norm counterexample in Proposition C.3, while omitting v1 Appendix C.3's explicit reward-to-decision equivalence derivation. Most earlier Chebyshev results are retained in Appendix C.

C1.justification: The quantitative framework and worst-case robustness remain the central scientific claims. v2 foregrounds general downstream decisions and one policy-preference algorithm, replacing the emphasis on selecting a reward and presenting three algorithms. Since the general decision formulation already appears in v1 Appendix C.3, this is a limited reframing of the advertised contributions.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly identifies Rob-ReL's restricted problem family as a limitation and explains the minimax choice through the absence of a prior distribution over rewards. The earlier discussion of insufficient feedback and the tradeoff between restrictive modeling assumptions and misspecification is largely retained, with model selection moved to Appendix D.

D1.justification: v2 Appendix F adds the laptop processor, 8 GB RAM and execution time of a few seconds. Algorithms 2–3 and Appendix E provide more explicit initialization, projection and visitation-recursion details. These additions improve documentation without establishing changed simulation settings.

R1.justification: v2 Appendix A substantially expands v1 Section 7, including comparisons with Viano et al.'s transition-robust IRL, Brown et al.'s Bayesian robust imitation and Cheng et al.'s noisy-preference method. It develops a detailed comparison with Skalse et al.'s qualitative framework and distinguishes identifiability robustness from other uncertainty settings. Some earlier references, including STARC, are removed.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction and main exposition are extensively rewritten. The general decision formulation moves from v1 Appendix C.3 into the main narrative; reward geometry, related work and model selection are reorganized into appendices. The algorithms are presented under Rob-ReL, and numerical simulations become a separate main section.

P2.justification: v2 replaces the two-column main layout with a single-column layout, expands the feedback table, adds an application/loss table and separates the optimization subroutines into pseudocode displays. Its main Figure 1 combines the existing road illustration and feasible-set plot, while the geometric schematic moves to Appendix C. The experimental appendix figures are largely retained and resized.

improvement.justification: v2 improves organization, research positioning, implementation documentation and treatment of sampled target policies. However, its new Appendix A.2 incorrectly recommends an equal mixture as minimax: for the displayed rewards and small Delta, its worst-case loss is 0.5, exceeding the pure first action's Delta. The simulation also retains signed values after reversing the return difference without explanation. These mathematical and reporting issues prevent a reliable net quality judgment.
